title: Indirect Statement (Accusative-Infinitive)
objectives: Choose correct infinitive tense (present, perfect, future)
Identify verbs that introduce indirect statement

grammar.explanation: After verbs of saying, thinking, knowing, perceiving, Latin uses an accusative subject + infinitive verb (not a 'that' clause). The infinitive tense shows time relative to the main verb: present = same time, perfect = earlier, future = later.

paradigms.name: Examples
rows: I say that he is coming
I said that he was coming
I say that he came/has come
I say that he will come

rules: Subject of infinitive = accusative (eum, eam, eos, etc.)
Reflexive (se) refers back to subject of main verb
Present infinitive = same time as main verb
Perfect infinitive = time before main verb
Future infinitive = time after main verb

exercises.question: Translate: Caesar dixit se vicisse.
exercises.answer: Caesar said that he had conquered.

exercises.question: Why 'se' not 'eum' in 'Caesar dixit se vicisse'?
exercises.answer: se refers back to Caesar (the subject of dixit); eum would mean someone else

readingPassage.latin: Nuntii dixerunt hostes adventare. Caesar credidit eos mox venturos esse. Milites sperabant se victoria potituros esse. Omnes sciebant bellum grave futurum esse.
readingPassage.translation: Messengers said that the enemy was approaching. Caesar believed that they would soon come. The soldiers hoped that they would gain victory. Everyone knew that the war would be serious.
notes: Note the different infinitive tenses expressing time relationships
